Penn enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 18-11 overall and 9-5 in Ivy League regular-season play, then added two Ivy League Tournament overtime wins—62-60 over Harvard on March 14, 2026 and 88-84 over Yale on March 15, 2026—to claim the automatic bid. The regular-season record and conference mark are listed on Penn’s official schedule page, which also shows the team carrying a five-game winning streak into the NCAA Tournament game against Illinois. Penn finished the regular season 12-2 at home, 4-8 on the road, and 2-1 on neutral courts. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/schedule/2025-26))

Offensively, this is a spacing-first, perimeter-forward Penn team built around TJ Power as the primary mismatch creator and Ethan Roberts as the volume scorer on the wing. Penn’s cumulative statistics show 76.2 points per game through the regular season at that snapshot, 44.2 percent team shooting, 38.2 percent from three, and only 10.9 turnovers per game, which tells you the identity clearly: spread the floor, hunt threes, and avoid empty trips. Power led the team with 77 made threes in 29 games, Roberts had 40 in 23 games, and Michael Zanoni added 53 in 29 games. That is not random shot-making; it is a roster built to put multiple above-average shooters on the floor at once. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025?utm_source=openai))

The named action Penn shows repeatedly is pick-and-roll and inside-out creation through Power/Roberts decision-making. In the January 5 loss at Princeton, Penn “worked a pick-and-roll with Scantlebury for an easy two” during a 9-0 run, a useful documented example of how McCaffery’s offense gets downhill before kicking out. In the March 15 Ivy title win over Yale, Penn made 14 threes on 28 attempts, its season high in made threes, which is the cleanest statistical proof of its preferred shot profile. In the February 27 win over Dartmouth, Power scored 38 on 14-of-22 shooting and 6-of-8 from three, and Penn attempted 37 free throws. Against Cornell on February 14, Penn took a season-high 41 free throws and made 27. So the full offensive picture is this: Penn wants threes first, but if defenders over-close, it will attack gaps and manufacture foul shots. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/news/2026/1/5/mens-basketball-falls-short-in-back-and-forth-game-at-princeton-78-76.aspx))

Penn’s offensive tendencies also show up in game-shape data. The Quakers are 8-1 when scoring at least 80 points, and they reached 80 in wins over Cornell twice, Dartmouth, Brown, and Yale in the Ivy final. On January 31 at Cornell, Penn posted season highs at that point in points (91), assists (20), and field-goal percentage (.556), with six double-figure scorers: Michael Zanoni 19, Ethan Roberts 17, AJ Levine 15, Augustus Gerhart 13, Dalton Scantlebury 12, and TJ Power 11. That game is the best evidence that when Penn can get into early offense and drive-kick rhythm, it becomes difficult to load up on any single scorer. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/news/2026/2/14/mens-basketball-outraces-cornell-again-this-time-82-76-at-the-palestra.aspx))

Defensively, Penn is more event-driven than purely stonewalling. The Quakers forced turnovers and converted them into offense in several defining wins. In the February 13 comeback against Columbia, Penn won the turnover game 20-10 and turned that into a 22-5 edge in points off turnovers, despite leading for only 2:46 of game time. In the March 6 win at Brown, Penn generated 19 steals, forced 23 turnovers, and scored 32 points off turnovers, all season-best type indicators. AJ Levine is the tone-setter here; by February 12 he already had 16 steals in Ivy play, tops in the league at that time. Penn’s late-game defensive philosophy also leans on ball pressure from Levine at the point of attack: in the February 7 win over Princeton, he blanketed Dalen Davis on the final possession and forced a contested fallaway that missed. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/news/2026/2/13/mens-basketball-roberts-leads-the-way-as-mens-hoops-comes-back-to-down-columbia-76-67.aspx))

That said, Penn is not a shutdown half-court defense in the classic sense. Opponents shot 45.3 percent against the Quakers in the regular-season cumulative stats, and the vulnerabilities show up against efficient, disciplined offenses. Princeton opened the second half of the January 5 game by making its first 18 shots across the field-goal/foul sequence stretch described in Penn’s recap and turned an eight-point halftime deficit into a 15-point lead. Yale beat Penn 77-60 on January 24 after responding immediately when Penn cut the margin to four. Providence hung 106 on the Quakers on November 11. So the defensive profile is aggressive hands, pressure on guards, and opportunistic runouts—but not elite rim deterrence. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025?utm_source=openai))

Fran McCaffery’s coaching philosophy is visible in how flexible Penn has been game to game. McCaffery historically coaches offense-first teams, and Penn’s shot mix, pace swings, and freedom for veteran scorers reflect that. The adjustment history is strong and documented. On February 28 versus Harvard, Penn erased a 10-point halftime deficit, its largest comeback at that point of the season; Roberts scored 21, with 17 after halftime, and Levine added 13, with 10 after halftime. One night earlier against Dartmouth, Penn overcame an eight-point halftime deficit; Power scored 38 and 22 of Penn’s first 36 second-half points. On March 14 in the Ivy semifinal, Penn won a grinder 62-60 over Harvard despite shooting only 40.3 percent and committing 17 turnovers; that was a tactical shift from its usual freer offensive style, and it survived because it held Harvard to 2-for-2 at the line and 8-for-31 from three. Then 24 hours later, McCaffery toggled back to spacing and shot-making: Penn beat Yale 88-84 with 14 made threes and Power exploding for 44 points. That two-day contrast—win ugly, then win with shotmaking—is strong evidence of coaching adaptability. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/news/2026/2/28/mens-basketball-comes-back-on-harvard-64-61-clinches-ivy-madness-bid.aspx))

Clutch and late-game execution is one of the strongest arguments for Penn as a dangerous underdog. On February 7, Penn beat Princeton 61-60, ending a 14-game losing streak in the series; the deciding sequence was defensive, with Levine smothering Princeton’s final shot. On February 28, Penn beat Harvard 64-61 to clinch an Ivy Madness berth after trailing by 10 at halftime. On March 14, Penn survived Harvard 62-60 in overtime, with AJ Levine hitting the game-winner in the extra period. On March 15, Penn beat Yale 88-84 in overtime for the title; Power had 44 points, Cam Thrower added 19, and Penn went 16-for-16 at the foul line. The other side of the ledger matters too: Penn lost 64-63 at Harvard on January 19 after a 54-54 tie with three minutes left, when Harvard scored on five straight possessions; Penn also lost 70-69 at Rutgers on December 20 on a buzzer-beater and 78-76 at Princeton on January 5 when Levine’s near-halfcourt three to win hit the back rim. So this is a team that has lived in one-possession games all year. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/news/2026/2/7/mens-basketball-mens-hoops-defends-home-court-edges-princeton-61-60.aspx))

The key players start with Power. He is the featured forward, the best shooter, and the rebound leader. For the full 29-game sample entering the tournament, he averaged 16.8 points and 7.5 rebounds, with 77 made threes and a 43.3 percent three-point rate. He posted 38 points and 12 rebounds against Dartmouth on February 27, then 44 points and 14 rebounds against Yale on March 15; the 44 tied for the third-highest scoring game in Penn history. He was also a unanimous first-team All-Ivy pick. Roberts is the tough-shot wing scorer: 16.9 points per game in 23 appearances, eight 20-point games, including 31 against Saint Joseph’s and 30 against Drexel. Against Harvard on January 19 he had 27 points on 9-of-15 shooting, and against Harvard on February 28 he scored 21, with 17 in the second half. Levine is the connective guard and defensive closer: 8.3 points per game overall, a team-high single-game 8 assists against Lafayette, 7 steals against NJIT, and the on-ball defense that sealed the February 7 Princeton win plus the overtime winner against Harvard on March 14. Zanoni is the secondary spacer at 11.6 points per game, 53 made threes, and a 91.7 percent free-throw rate in the earlier cumulative sample; he scored 19 at Cornell in one of Penn’s best offensive games. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025))

The notable wins reveal exactly what Penn can be. Saint Joseph’s, 83-74 on November 17, showed Roberts’ star-level ceiling; he later was credited with a 31-point outing in that game. The January 31 road win at Cornell, 91-81, showed Penn’s best five-out flow and scoring balance. The February 7 Princeton win, 61-60, showed composure in a rock fight. The February 14 Cornell win, 82-76, highlighted Penn’s ability to weaponize foul pressure with 41 free-throw attempts. The March 15 Yale win, 88-84 in overtime, proved Penn can beat the league’s best team with star power. The losses are equally revealing: Providence 106-81 exposed transition and containment issues against high-major athletes; Yale 77-60 on January 24 showed Penn struggling when a disciplined favorite answered every push; Harvard 64-63 on January 19 and Rutgers 70-69 on December 20 showed that late-game possessions can still bog down if Power/Roberts are crowded. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/schedule/2025-26))

As for McCaffery’s NCAA Tournament history, Penn’s official bio says he has coached 12 teams to NCAA Tournament appearances. Those appearances span Lehigh in 1988, UNC Greensboro in 2001, Siena in 2008, 2009, and 2010, and Iowa in 2014, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2021, 2022, and 2023. As a Penn player, he also played in the NCAA Tournament in 1980 and 1982. In terms of rounds reached as a head coach, the documented pattern is Round of 64 exits with Lehigh and UNC Greensboro, Round of 32 trips with Siena in 2008 and 2009, another Round of 64 trip with Siena in 2010, and Iowa appearances that never advanced to the Sweet 16. That matters in scouting terms: McCaffery has a long history of getting teams to March, several examples of first-round wins, but no documented Sweet 16 breakthrough as a head coach. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/fran-mccaffery/4650?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Penn is not a fluky bid stealer. The Quakers are an experienced, shot-making, late-game-tested team whose identity is clear—Power as the matchup warper, Roberts as the scoring wing, Levine as the defensive pressure guard, Zanoni as the extra floor spacer. They are vulnerable if opponents finish efficiently inside the arc and keep Penn out of transition, but if the game becomes a three-point and free-throw contest, this is the kind of 18-11 Ivy champion that can play above its seed line for 40 minutes. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025))
forecaster:
Penn enters the 2026 tournament conversation as a classic mid-major analytic split case: good enough to look respectable in broad résumé systems, but not strong enough in underlying efficiency to project as a real bracket disruptor without a favorable draw. The clearest current anchors I could verify are Penn’s NCAA NET rank of 139, ESPN BPI rank of 190, and Warren Nolan NET strength-of-schedule rank of 183, with a non-conference SOS rank of 232. ESPN’s Ivy BPI page listed Penn at 16-12 with a BPI of about -1.6, an offensive component of -1.0, and a defensive component of -0.6 as of March 11, 2026. Those values frame Penn as roughly a lower-middle tier national team rather than a true at-large caliber profile. Sports-Reference’s 2025-26 Penn team page also surfaced a defensive rating of 105.0, ranked 138th nationally. Meanwhile, Ivy Hoops Online reported Penn sitting 123rd nationally in defensive efficiency on KenPom entering the Ivy League tournament. Taken together, the market signal is that Penn’s defense is materially better than public perception, while the offense is more ordinary than the team’s best scoring nights suggest.

The most important divergence in Penn’s profile is between résumé rank and predictive rank. A 139 NET is meaningfully better than a 190 BPI. That gap usually signals a team that banked a decent number of wins, probably avoided catastrophic losses too often, and played more competitively than its pure possession-level strength would indicate. Penn’s schedule/results page shows a season with enough solid wins to keep the résumé afloat: victories over Saint Joseph’s, Drexel, La Salle, Hofstra, Princeton, Cornell, Dartmouth, Harvard, Brown, and Columbia, plus a close one-point road loss at Rutgers and several competitive Ivy games. But the same record line also shows Penn was not consistently beating the better teams on its schedule, with losses to Providence, Villanova, George Mason, Yale, Princeton on the road, and Columbia on the road. That is the profile of a team that can win its league tournament but is not carrying hidden top-75 national strength.

On raw possession efficiency, the accessible numbers suggest Penn is around break-even to modestly positive overall. If Sports-Reference’s team defensive rating is 105.0 and BPI pegs the offense and defense both slightly below national average in opponent-adjusted terms, the likely interpretation is that Penn’s unadjusted offensive efficiency sat somewhere in the low 100s per 100 possessions and its defense around 105 allowed per 100 possessions, with schedule adjustment moving those figures modestly. Ivy Hoops Online’s note that Penn ranked 123rd in KenPom defensive efficiency is significant: that is comfortably better than the eye-test stereotype attached to a Fran McCaffery team. Conventional wisdom tends to assume McCaffery teams are offense-first and porous defensively; the available 2026 data says Penn’s defense was the more credible half of the team. The offense, not the defense, appears to be the limiting variable.

Pace is harder to pin down exactly from open sources, but the season shape suggests Penn is not playing extreme Ivy slowball. Game logs show frequent scores in the 70s and 80s, including 84-68 at Drexel, 83-74 over Saint Joseph’s, 81-73 over Brown, 84-74 at Dartmouth, 91-81 at Cornell, 82-76 over Cornell, 80-71 over Dartmouth, and 82-61 at Brown. That scoring environment implies at least a moderate tempo rather than a grind-it-down possession count in the low 60s. I would characterize Penn as closer to average pace than to either extreme: willing to play fluidly, not relentlessly fast, but not trying to win 58-54 games either. The scoring profile and McCaffery imprint both point in that direction.

The shot-profile evidence is clearer than the exact Four Factors table. Penn’s game logs repeatedly show healthy three-point volume: 21 attempts at American, 28 at Providence, 12 vs. Merrimack, and multiple later games with double-digit makes. That strongly suggests a meaningful 3-point attempt rate, likely above national average. The offense appears to lean on perimeter creation and spacing more than brute-force interior efficiency. The upside is obvious: Penn can generate shot variance and punch above its baseline when perimeter players get hot. The downside is that teams with middling adjusted offense and high jump-shot dependence often look better in box-score bursts than they do in stable predictive models. That helps explain why Penn can produce an eye-catching win or two without earning top-100 predictive respect.

On shooting efficiency, the scattered box-score evidence suggests Penn is decent but not elite. The offense has had several high-eFG nights, especially in wins, but also some real crash-outs against stronger defenses. Against Merrimack, Penn posted a .560 eFG. Against American it was .510; against Providence just .443. Those early logs summarize the larger pattern well: good enough shooting to function, not good enough to insulate the team against step-up competition when the first action is taken away. Because the offense is probably more perimeter-oriented, Penn’s eFG% may look respectable in wins yet remain fragile against long, athletic opponents who can contest above the arc and switch actions without fouling.

Turnover behavior appears mixed but not disastrous. In the early logs Penn had 17 turnovers at American, a cleaner 10 at Providence despite the blowout, and 11 against Merrimack. Ivy Hoops Online also highlighted defensive ball pressure as a key tactical lever, implying Penn’s own defense can manufacture some extra possessions. That matters because if the offense is only moderately efficient, Penn needs hidden-possession edges from steals, transition leaks, and avoiding empty trips. Offensive rebounding and free-throw generation are less directly documented in the searchable material, but the available game logs do show Penn capable of drawing fouls in volume on some nights, such as 32 free-throw attempts at American and 24 at Providence. That suggests the team is not purely reliant on jumpers; there is at least some downhill pressure built into the offense.

Recent form is quietly encouraging. Penn closed with wins over Dartmouth, Harvard, and Brown, and split late-season meetings with Princeton and Yale competitively. The final stretch looks better than the full-season reputation: the Quakers were more coherent defensively and more reliable in close games than earlier in the year. That does not necessarily mean their last-10 efficiency trend exploded upward into top-100 territory, but it does suggest improvement relative to their early-season baseline. In forecasting terms, Penn looks like a team whose end-of-season version is stronger than the average of its full sample.

The cleanest synthesis is this: Penn is not a secretly elite team hiding behind an Ivy label, but it is also not the soft, offense-only group casual observers might assume. The résumé metrics are decent, the predictive metrics are skeptical, and the defense is better than brand perception. The likely true talent level is that of a roughly top-140 to top-180 team nationally, with enough three-point volume and competent defense to be dangerous in a one-bid conference tournament, but not enough adjusted offensive punch or schedule-tested dominance to project as more than a live underdog in the NCAA field. If Penn makes the bracket, the upset path would come from hitting threes, keeping turnovers manageable, and leaning on a defense that has outperformed the eye test all season.
matchup-analyst:
Penn enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a clear offense-first, spacing-heavy team whose identity is built around shooting and half-court scoring from its frontcourt wings. The baseline numbers are blunt: Penn averages 76.1 points per game, shoots 44.0% from the field, 38.6% from three, and only turns it over 10.8 times per game. Four players average at least 8.3 points, led by Ethan Roberts at 16.9, TJ Power at 16.8, Michael Zanoni at 11.6, and AJ Levine at 8.3 assists/turnover hub duties. The biggest tactical tell is shot profile by personnel: Power has taken 178 threes in 29 games and made 43.3%, Roberts has taken 99 and made 40.4%, and Zanoni has taken 136 and made 39.0%, so Penn is not just willing to shoot over the top of coverage; it is structurally designed to do so through multiple 6-5 to 6-9 perimeter-sized scorers. That makes the first rule simple: run them off clean catch-and-shoot rhythm and force secondary creators to finish possessions inside the arc. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025))

Penn’s style is most disruptive when it can play with balanced spacing, use Power as a stretch-4 mismatch, and let Roberts attack closeouts or late-clock situations. Their best evidence games are ones where the floor is spread and several scorers contribute: at Cornell on January 31, Penn scored a season-high 91 points, shot 30-for-54 overall, posted a season-best 20 assists, and had six players in double figures; against Saint Joseph’s on November 17, Roberts scored 31 and Penn won 83-74; against Dartmouth on January 17, Power had 27 and Roberts 25 in an 84-74 win while Penn shot 9-for-21 from three. Those games show the template: if opponents cannot flatten the spacing or top-lock shooters, Penn’s offense becomes very difficult to guard for a full 40. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/news/2026/2/1/mens-basketball-mens-hoops-starts-strong-holds-off-cornell-rally-for-91-81-road-win.aspx?utm_source=openai))

The tactics that disrupt Penn are specific. First, speed them up defensively without necessarily pressing for steals every possession; Penn wants to be efficient, not chaotic. Second, switch size onto the shooting forwards and make them finish through length at the rim. Third, attack Penn’s defense before it is set. The clearest punishment games came against higher-end athletes: Providence beat Penn 106-81 on November 11, and Villanova beat Penn 90-63 on December 6. In both games Penn still made 11 threes, which is important: the issue was not that Penn could not generate jumpers, but that those opponents won the game with superior physicality, pace control, and overall shot quality. Providence’s transition edge was especially telling; Penn was outscored 26-4 in fast-break points in that game, a direct indicator that Penn can be hurt badly when the game becomes a sprint instead of a half-court shooting contest. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/news/2025/11/12/mens-basketball-can-t-keep-up-wiih-providence-falls-106-81.aspx))

On press vulnerability, there is mixed evidence. The season-long turnover data says Penn is relatively secure: just 10.8 turnovers per game against opponents forcing only 12.5, and in conference play Penn averaged 12.4 turnovers while opponents averaged 14.5. Penn also had only five turnovers against Dartmouth on January 17 and just eight in the 83-79 loss to George Mason on December 28. That suggests full-court pressure is not automatically a winning formula if it merely extends the game. The better use of pressure is selective: trap after makes, deny the first reversal, then force AJ Levine to become a scorer instead of an organizer. Levine averages 4.0 assists but also 57 turnovers, and he is only a 29.0% three-point shooter overall and 16.7% from three in Ivy play, so going under him and loading gaps is defensible. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025))

Zone vulnerability is harder to prove conclusively from public 2026 data, but the available evidence points to a team that generally punishes soft zone with shooting rather than one that struggles against it. Penn entered January 10 ranked 15th nationally in three-point percentage at 39.1%, and by season end remained at 38.6%. They made 11 threes against Providence, 11 against Villanova, 9 against Dartmouth on January 17, and 7-for-16 against Brown on January 10. So a passive 2-3 zone is unlikely to work. If you zone Penn, it has to be an extended, matchup-style zone that crowds Power and Roberts above the break and concedes post touches to non-primary finishers. The public evidence does not show a named game where standard zone alone broke Penn’s offense; the stronger inference is that length plus ball pressure is what bothered them, not coverage shell by itself. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/news/2026/1/10/mens-basketball-holds-off-brown-for-first-ivy-win-81-73.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Preferred pace: Penn is better when the game is controlled and efficient, with its half-court shooting allowed to accumulate. Even external analysis during the season tagged Penn as a relatively faster Ivy team at roughly 72 possessions, but their best wins still read like structured offensive games, not pure track meets. Their defense improved notably after New Year’s according to Ivy Hoops Online and BartTorvik/KenPom references, but the nonconference blowout losses show that against high-major speed and athleticism Penn’s defensive floor drops. To force the opposite, opponents should rebound-and-run off every miss, push on makes when possible, and hunt early drag screens against Penn’s bigger forwards before matchups are set. Providence’s 26-4 fast-break edge is the clearest example; Villanova’s 90 points on Penn in a 27-point win is the second. ([ivyhoopsonline.com](https://ivyhoopsonline.com/2026/03/01/quakeaways-from-penn-mens-basketballs-sweep-of-dartmouth-and-harvard/?utm_source=openai))

Position-by-position mismatch map: at point guard, 6-0 AJ Levine is a good rebounder for his size but can be shot over by bigger lead guards; his value is playmaking and steals, not shot creation from deep. At the 2/3, Penn has real size with 6-5 Roberts and 6-5 Zanoni, both strong shooters, but neither is an overwhelming rim athlete; long, switchable wings can crowd their airspace. At the 4, 6-9 TJ Power is the marquee mismatch creator because he shoots 43.3% from three on huge volume while also averaging 7.9 rebounds; if defended by a slow big, he spaces and drives, but if defended by a strong lateral forward he can be pushed into tougher two-point attempts. At the 5, Penn is functional but not dominant: 6-9 Augustus Gerhart averages 5.6 points and 4.8 rebounds, while reserve 6-9/250 Dalton Scantlebury gives 6.0 points and 4.0 rebounds in 15.6 minutes. Penn’s shot-blocking is modest at 3.1 per game while opponents average 3.8, so an explosive rim-running center can stress them on both ends. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mbball/roster))

Isolation versus team offense: Penn is primarily a team-offense shooting group, not an isolation-heavy attack. The proof is structural rather than proprietary Synergy labels: 405 assists on 766 made field goals means 52.9% of Penn’s baskets were assisted. In conference play it was 173 assists on 360 makes, 48.1%. That is too high for an iso-dependent team. The late-clock bailout is Roberts, and the matchup piece is Power, but the offense overall is more reversal, spacing, and spot-up creation than repeated clear-outs. When Penn is humming, the ball moves: 20 assists at Cornell, 19 assists against George Mason, and a 1.3 season assist/turnover ratio. Therefore, switching plus top-side denial is more effective than loading up for one-on-one containment alone. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025))

Transition offense and defense: Penn can score in flow, but the public 2026 evidence says transition defense is the more actionable weakness. The Providence game is the headline datapoint: Penn scored only four fast-break points while allowing 26. On the other side, Penn’s own defense-generated offense can spike against weak handlers; in the March 6 win at Brown, Penn had 19 steals, forced 23 turnovers, and scored 32 points off those turnovers, all season highs against Division I competition. That means Penn can be dangerous in transition when its pressure creates live-ball events, but against NCAA-level backcourts the more predictive trait is vulnerability to opponent pace and athleticism in the open floor. ([inquirer.com](https://www.inquirer.com/college-sports/penn/penn-quakers-providence-mbb-ivy-league-20251112.html?utm_source=openai))

Coaching adaptability: this is Fran McCaffery’s first Penn season, so there is no true NCAA “mid-series” sample with this roster, but the season does show midgame adjustment evidence. Penn came back to beat Columbia on February 13 despite leading only 2:46 total; Roberts scored 14 in the final five minutes. Penn also flipped a 10-point halftime deficit against Harvard on February 28 into a 64-61 win to clinch its Ivy Madness berth, and on February 7 it slowed Princeton into a 61-60 grinder after losing the first meeting 78-76. Those are legitimate examples that this staff can change game texture from one segment to the next: from trailing to closing, from offense-first to possession-by-possession defense. That said, the same staff did not solve the athletic-gap games against Providence, Villanova, or Yale, so adaptability looks better inside Ivy-level talent bands than against superior physical rosters. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/news/2026/2/13/mens-basketball-roberts-leads-the-way-as-mens-hoops-comes-back-to-down-columbia-76-67.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Penn you must 1) sprint them into defensive cross-matches and attack before Power/Gerhart are set, 2) top-lock Roberts and Zanoni off spot-up threes, 3) switch a mobile 6-7 to 6-9 defender onto Power and force him to finish over bodies instead of shooting pick-and-pop threes, 4) go under Levine and pack gaps because he is a 29.0% three-point shooter overall and 16.7% in Ivy play, 5) use selective pressure rather than constant gambling, because Penn only gives it away 10.8 times per game, and 6) punish the rim where Penn is smaller and less explosive than its perimeter skill suggests. If you let Penn play a clean, rhythmic half-court game, its 38.6% team three-point shooting and multi-forward spacing can beat you. If you make it a speed-and-size game, the evidence from Providence, Villanova, and Yale says Penn becomes vulnerable fast. ([pennathletics.com](https://pennathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025))
